population_segments.name: Older Adults with Intermediate or Complex Health
Older Adults at the End of Life

specific_goals.name: Glycemic goals for older adults with few and stable coexisting chronic illnesses, and intact cognitive and functional status
specific_goals.source_text: lower glycemic goals (such as A1C <7.0–7.5% [<53–58 mmol/mol]) and/or time in range [TIR] 70–180 mg/dL [3.9–10.0 mmol/L] of ≥70% and time below range ≤70 mg/dL [≤3.9 mmol/L] of ≤4%) if CGM is used.
specific_goals.rationale: few and stable coexisting chronic illnesses, and intact cognitive and functional status

specific_goals.name: Glycemic goals for older adults with intermediate or complex health
specific_goals.source_text: less stringent goals (such as A1C <8.0% [<64 mmol/mol] and/or TIR 70–180 mg/dL [3.9–10.0 mmol/L] of ≥50% and time below range).
specific_goals.rationale: intermediate or complex health, clinically heterogeneous with variable life expectancy. Selection of glycemic goals should be individualized and should prioritize avoidance of hypoglycemia

specific_goals.name: Glycemic goals for older adults with complex or intermediate health and shorter life expectancy
specific_goals.rationale: shorter life expectancy, advanced diabetes complications, life-limiting comorbid illnesses, frailty, or substantial cognitive or functional impairments

specific_goals.name: Glycemic goals for older adults at the end of life
specific_goals.source_text: avoid hypoglycemia and symptomatic hyperglycemia while reducing the burdens of glycemic management.

specific_goals.name: Glucose goal for community-dwelling individuals receiving short-term care in a skilled nursing facility
specific_goals.rationale: Recovery from acute illness may impair cognitive function

specific_goals.name: Glycemic goal for very complex/poor health individuals (PALTC or end-stage chronic illnesses or moderate to severe cognitive impairment or ≥2 ADL impairments)
specific_goals.source_text: avoid reliance on A1C and avoid hypoglycemia
specific_goals.target_value: Avoid reliance on A1C and avoid hypoglycemia
specific_goals.rationale: No benefits of tight glycemic goals in this population. Most important outcomes are maintenance of cognitive and functional status

specific_goals.name: Glycemic goal for individuals at the end of life
specific_goals.source_text: avoid hypoglycemia (blood glucose <70 mg/dL) and severe hyperglycemia (blood glucose >250 mg/dL when symptom burden increases)
specific_goals.target_value: Avoid hypoglycemia (<70 mg/dL) and severe hyperglycemia (>250 mg/dL)
specific_goals.rationale: prioritize symptom management and quality of life

allowed_medications.name: Metformin for older adults with type 2 diabetes
allowed_medications.source_text: Metformin is a good treatment option for glucose lowering in older adults with type 2 diabetes due to its low risk for hypoglycemia and simple administration profile
allowed_medications.special_instructions: May be used safely in individuals with an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) ≥30 mL/min/1.73 m²; lower doses should be used in those with eGFR 30–45 mL/min/1.73 m². eGFR should be monitored every 3–6 months. Contraindicated in those with advanced kidney disease. Use with caution in those with hypoperfusion, hypoxemia, and impaired hepatic function. Can cause gastrointestinal side effects. Extended-release formulation may be used as an alternative. Monitor vitamin B12 levels annually for those taking metformin long term (>4 years).

allowed_medications.name: DPP-4 Inhibitors for older adults
allowed_medications.source_text: DPP-4 inhibitors have few side effects and minimal risk of hypoglycemia
allowed_medications.special_instructions: May be useful in older adults with mild hyperglycemia or with high risk of hypoglycemia when a GLP-1 RA or a dual GIP/GLP-1 RA is not tolerated.

allowed_medications.name: Pioglitazone for older adults
allowed_medications.source_text: Pioglitazone has low risk for hypoglycemia
allowed_medications.special_instructions: Should be used cautiously and in select individuals due to risks for heart failure, fluid retention, weight gain, osteoporosis, and/or macular edema. Adverse effect risks are reduced with lower doses and when used as part of combination therapy.

allowed_medications.name: GLP-1 RAs for older adults
allowed_medications.source_text: GLP-1 RAs and the GIP/GLP-1 RA tirzepatide are highly effective glucose-lowering agents.
allowed_medications.special_instructions: Injectable agents (except oral semaglutide) require visual, motor, and cognitive skills for administration. May be associated with nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and/or constipation; doses should be titrated slowly. Not preferred in older adults experiencing unexplained weight loss or undernutrition or with problematic constipation, significant gastroparesis, recurrent ileus, or bowel obstruction. Monitor regularly for dehydration and excessive weight loss.

allowed_medications.name: SGLT2 Inhibitors for older adults
allowed_medications.source_text: SGLT2 inhibitors are generally well tolerated among older adults
allowed_medications.special_instructions: May cause clinically significant volume depletion; use cautiously in older adults who are frail or prone to orthostasis. May cause a higher rate of genital mycotic infections. May be associated with a small increase in urinary tract infections. Symptoms of urinary incontinence should be queried before and after initiation. Euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) is a rare but potentially serious phenomenon.

allowed_medications.name: Basal insulin for older adults with Type 1 Diabetes
allowed_medications.source_text: Insulin is an essential life-preserving therapy for people with type 1 diabetes. To avoid DKA, older adults with type 1 diabetes need some form of basal insulin even when they are unable to ingest meals.
allowed_medications.special_instructions: May be delivered through injection, with an AID system, or with an insulin pump alone. CGM should be used in conjunction with any insulin delivery system.

allowed_medications.name: Oral agents for older adults with Type 2 Diabetes at end of life
allowed_medications.source_text: Pharmacologic therapy for type 2 diabetes may include oral agents with low likelihood of causing hypoglycemia as first line
allowed_medications.medication_name: Oral agents with low likelihood of causing hypoglycemia
allowed_medications.special_instructions: As symptoms progress, some agents may be slowly tapered and discontinued.

allowed_medications.name: Basal insulin for older adults with Type 2 Diabetes at end of life
allowed_medications.source_text: followed by a simplified insulin plan such as basal insulin.
allowed_medications.special_instructions: As symptoms progress, some agents may be slowly tapered and discontinued.

contraindicated_medications.name: Glyburide for older adults
contraindicated_medications.source_text: Glyburide is a longer-acting sulfonylurea with multiple active metabolites and should be avoided in older adults due to its hypoglycemia risk
contraindicated_medications.alternative: sulfonylureas with a shorter duration of action, such as glipizide

contraindicated_medications.name: Metformin in advanced kidney disease
contraindicated_medications.source_text: metformin is contraindicated in those with advanced kidney disease
